scenario.context: A food-discovery startup wants to understand how people decide where to eat on a weeknight.

steps.task: Write 3 learning goals and 8 open questions in a sensible order, and list 2 questions to avoid.
hints: Ask about the last time, not what they usually do.

goals: Learn what criteria and frustrations shape the choice.

questions.label: Warm-up
questions.text: Tell me a bit about your usual weeknight.
Tell me about the last time you ate out or ordered in on a weeknight.
Walk me through it from the moment you felt hungry.
How did you decide where to go?
What other options did you consider?
Was there anything that nearly changed your mind or made it harder?
Who else was involved, and how did they influence it?

questions.label: Wrap-up
questions.text: If you could change one thing about how you decide, what would it be? Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

avoid.text: Would you use an app that recommends restaurants?

reference.whyItWorks: The guide moves from context to a specific past event to depth and a wrap-up.

scenario.context: An invoicing startup wants to learn why freelancers get paid late. The founder tends to pitch the product during interviews.

steps.task: Write a guide with warm-up, past-behaviour, depth and wrap-up sections (9 to 10 questions), add 3 follow-up probes, and list 3 questions to avoid and why.
hints: Focus on the last late payment.
Probes should dig into what happened, not into opinions.

questions.label: Warm-up
questions.text: What kind of work do you do, and how do you find clients?

questions.label: Warm-up
questions.text: How do you usually get paid?

questions.label: Past behaviour
questions.text: Tell me about the last invoice that was paid late.

questions.label: Past behaviour
questions.text: What happened from sending it until it was paid?

questions.label: Past behaviour
questions.text: What did you do when it was late?

questions.label: Depth
questions.text: How do you decide when to follow up?

questions.label: Depth
questions.text: What tools or notes do you use?

questions.label: Depth
questions.text: How did the client react?

questions.label: Depth
questions.text: What does a late payment cost you?

questions.label: Wrap-up
questions.text: What is the hardest part of getting paid? Anything else I should know?

probes: Can you tell me more about that?
What did you expect to happen?

avoid.text: Would you use a tool that sends automatic reminders?
How often are you paid late?
avoid.why: Asks them to average; answers will be unreliable.

reference.whyItWorks: Focuses on a real recent event so answers show actual behaviour and cost.
rubric: Focus on a specific recent event

scenario.context: An edtech company is building a learning app for children aged 8 to 12. Parents buy it and children use it. Parents may feel guilty about screen time and give socially desirable answers.

steps.task: Write a guide for parent interviews, explain how you will reduce socially desirable answers, and plan an ethical way to learn from children.

goals: How they discovered and chose learning apps, who influenced the decision, what they track, and what makes them cancel.

questions.text: Tell me about the last learning app or paid course you chose for your child.
How did you find it?
What else did you look at?
Who was involved in the decision?
What happened in the first week?
How do you know whether your child is learning?
Tell me about a time you stopped using one.
How do you handle screen time on a typical day?

approach: Avoid moral language about screen time.
Ask what they did, not what they should do.
children: Only with parental consent and the child's own agreement.
Ask about favourite activities, not about the product's quality.
The child can stop at any time.

avoid.text: Do you limit screen time enough?
avoid.why: Moral wording that triggers defensive answers.

reference.whyItWorks: Treats buyer and user differently and builds consent and bias controls into the method.
commonMistakes: Moral wording that triggers defensive answers
